extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially fantasy/sci‑fi/historical) writing warfare, combat scenes, or weaponry
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for crafting believable, engaging depictions of warfare, combat, and weapons in fiction — from small skirmishes to large battles — including research, perspective, and how to invent non‑technological weapons for a setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: If in doubt, make it a character mistake
rubrics_metrics.description: If you think it may be wrong, let it be a character who can make a mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fallibility as a shield: attribute tactical errors to an individual character's ignorance or bad judgement rather than presenting poor tactics as universal correctness. Anti-pattern: writing 'super soldiers' who always get everything right without doing a lot of homework — that will be picked apart by knowledgeable readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research extensively (talk to experienced people)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay attention (reading or listening) to people who 'have seen the elephant.' Talk to somebody who has been there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek out veterans, police, or others with direct experience and use them as alpha/beta readers to catch emotional and tactical inaccuracies. Example: the hosts send drafts to police/soldiers to correct tactics and emotional portrayal. Scoring note: realism improves with primary accounts and specialist review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use online communities and re-enactment footage for practical reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Use YouTube historicals and recreations (BazBattles, Lindybeige, Shadiversity, HEMA demonstrations) to see tactics and weapon use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watching multiple bouts or recreations shows repeated outcomes and helps you visualize how fights play out (e.g., 20 bouts in a row). Use battlefield tours/documentaries to understand terrain effects on tactics. Anti-pattern: relying only on secondhand summaries; prefer visual/firsthand demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make it personal — focus on characters' experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Make it very, very personal. Give us someone to care about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with large‑scale war, center the narrative on a handful of characters so readers have a point of identification (examples: War Horse, The Girl with All the Gifts). Detail small human concerns (logistics, socks) to convey authenticity. Avoid taking the lens so far back that no one is empathetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the lens tight / limit viewpoint during combat
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the lens tight, and focus on a few characters, even if the landscape is very wide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staying in one character's head during chaos (example: Django Wexler infantry sequence) preserves immediacy and prevents confusion. Anti-pattern: switching to broad omniscient perspectives mid-battle so the audience doesn't know who to root for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust technical detail to audience (young readers vs adults)
rubrics_metrics.description: For young readers, you don’t have to get that technical; make it personal rather than tactical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor how much procedural/tactical accuracy you present depending on reader expectations and age. Young‑reader fiction can prioritize emotional stakes over complex military detail without losing effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use extrapolation and purposeful alteration (wildcards) in speculative settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use extrapolation, add elements of technology, magic, or combat that change the way the game is played. Add wildcards to make it your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately change or invent elements (shard blades, impossible chasms, starship tech) so the warfare differs enough from real history that readers can accept it. This reduces the burden of absolute realism while allowing specialist readers to enjoy the premise. Also use these changes to justify unconventional tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: When inventing a weapon, consider societal and battlefield adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Invent a powerful, NON-technological weapon for your setting and see how society adapts to it; build a battlefield around the idea of a weapon no one fully understands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think beyond the weapon's immediate effect: how would tactics, logistics, politics, and daily life change? Make the weapon influence strategy, culture, and the physical layout of conflicts. Homework exercise recommended by hosts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get the emotions right by reading/listening to veterans' accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: There’s an aspect to soldiering that no one who has not soldiered can really understand — a blend of adrenaline, esprit de corps, fright and thrill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid writing feelings soldiers wouldn't have, read widely and listen to first‑person accounts; use those to shape your point‑of‑view descriptions. Beta readers with service experience can flag emotional inaccuracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small, mundane details to convey realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Soldier stories often revolve around mundane, logistic concerns rather than grand battles (example: supply sergeant stories about finding socks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including trivial but specific details (logistics, boredom, waiting, lack of supplies) grounds large events and creates believable texture. These details can show day‑to‑day reality rather than constant combat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid self-deprecating or intentionally nonsensical military jokes repeatedly
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t repeatedly poke fun at your ignorance by making ranks and forms of battle intentionally nonsensical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such jokes wear thin; instead, research and correct early errors. If you must lampoon ignorance, use it sparingly and knowingly as a character trait, not as an ongoing excuse for factual sloppiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrapolate transferable human dynamics from non-military experience
rubrics_metrics.description: You can extrapolate military‑like human behavior from other hierarchical, high‑pressure environments (e.g., dysfunctional corporate management).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you lack direct military experience, use analogous real‑world settings you do know to model command structures, bad decisions, and human reactions under stress. This helps plausibly portray human behavior in conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use terrain and site study to inform tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Visiting or studying battle sites (hills, positions) gives a sense of how terrain affected tactics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentaries and site tours can help you accurately place forces and explain decisions of historical commanders. Anti-pattern: ignoring terrain and inventing implausible troop placements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on repetitive demonstrations to see likely outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Watching repeated reenactments or bouts (e.g., HEMA matches) shows how situations play out multiple times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing variability and common patterns in several trials helps you write more believable fight choreography and avoid one-off unrealistic outcomes. Use video libraries to view many iterations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Super‑competent characters require deeper homework
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are writing somebody as a super soldier who tactically gets everything right, you have to do a whole lot more homework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert characters will be scrutinized by knowledgeable readers; provide plausible training, doctrine, and reasoning to justify near‑perfect performance. Otherwise, attribute competence to plot devices or explicit training background.
